title: The Premise Is the Problem:Exchangeability Failure in Self-Monitored Test-Time Adaptation

paper.title: The Premise Is the Problem: Exchangeability Failure in Self-Monitored Test-Time Adaptation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Modern forecasting models are often updated after deployment so they can respond to changing data.
These updates can also make predictions worse, so practical systems need a reliable monitor that
can detect harmful changes and trigger protection. A natural design is to monitor the same
prediction errors that guide the updates. This paper asks whether the statistical guarantee behind
such a monitor remains valid when monitoring and adaptation use the same feedback. We study this
question in multi-step time-series forecasting. We show that overlapping targets and dependence in
forecast errors can break a key assumption required by the guarantee. The monitor may then raise
alarms even when no harmful change has occurred, and its response can further damage prediction
quality. We also find that adaptation can hide sustained changes from its own monitor, while the
original frozen model retains a clearer signal. These results expose a basic failure mode in
self-monitored adaptation. They show why reliable deployment requires checking the monitor’s
assumptions, comparing adaptation with the frozen model under realistic feedback, and limiting the
effect of every protective response.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Self-monitored adaptation and the label-reuse mechanism; the stream is illustrative and the callouts summarize Section 4.3 . Consecutive 96-step labels share 95 of their 96 entries, so the oracle score is a moving sum. On a conditional null with the scorer held at the truth, reuse changes the classical no-reset wealth process from 2 or 3 of 60 crossings to 58 or 59 of 60; the Ville guarantee applies only when fresh labels are used. Appendix A specifies every component. Time-series foundation models forecast many steps ahead and are deployed frozen ( Auer et al., 2025 ; Ansari et al., 2025 ; Das et al., 2024 ) . Test-time adaptation corrects their forecasts from newly revealed labels ( Lee et al., 2025b ; Dai et al., 2026 ) , but learning from a corrupted or shifting stream can cause harm. Such an adaptive system therefore needs a monitor for protective action. Conformal test martingales offer an appealing guarantee for such a monitor. On an exchangeable score sequence the wealth crosses 1 / α \nicefrac{{1}}{{\alpha}} with probability at most α \alpha , uniformly in time. The adapter’s own scores are a readily available monitoring signal, so the natural design lets one score stream both drive the updates and police them (Figure 1 ). We call this self-monitored adaptation. This paper asks whether the guarantee survives that feedback loop. The question matters because the bounded probability of any false alarm is the reason to prefer such a gate over a heuristic threshold. A false alarm can trigger a response that damages the adapter. We study a block Kalman adapter applied to three frozen backbones: TiRex, Chronos-2, and TimesFM 2.5. We evaluate it on five public streams: ETTh2, ETTm1, weather, electricity, and traffic ( Zhou et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2021 ) . The main campaign uses immediate and delayed reveal. Targeted analyses use composite coordinate and stride-96 feedback. We count fires on clean replay and under injected contamination, separate the elements of the loop with synthetic nulls, replay the classical growing-calibration, no-reset wealth process on saved scores, build a conditional null that changes only the reuse of labels across overlapping horizons, and evaluate the adapter against the frozen backbone under deployable feedback. Because the deployed gate’s sliding calibration window and wealth resets make it heuristic, the classical replay is its formal audit. We recorded a decision rule before running each campaign. Later response, fallback, and frozen-residual studies were exploratory follow-ups and are labeled as such. We report every outcome, including a failed first design, and connect a classical dependence pattern to the loss of validity that occurs when an exact sequential test is applied outside its exchangeability null, and to damage from the resulting response. We make four contributions. • Failure of the statistical premise. We prove that reusing overlapping forecast labels can make even a correctly specified score sequence non-exchangeable, so the classical anytime-valid guarantee does not apply. In a controlled null, reuse raises crossings from 2 or 3 of 60 to 58 or 59 of 60; spacing origins one horizon apart restores validity for the truth-held scorer (Section 4 ; Appendix D ). • Evidence on real streams. Frozen-backbone residuals also cross without a learner, so adaptation is not necessary for the observed alarms. Using disjoint forecast origins greatly reduces crossings, but this real-stream comparison is descriptive and does not establish a Ville bound (Section 4.3 ; Appendix D ). • Value and limits of adaptation. The adapter absorbs a sustained change within one horizon, while the frozen residual remains elevated and can support later detection. Under two deployable feedback protocols, however, the adapter loses to the frozen backbone in 29 of 30 backbone–stream evaluations (Section 6 ). • Consequences of intervention. Detecting a change and responding safely are separate problems. The tested responses can reproduce divergence, act too often on clean data, or fail under sustained contamination; removing reset and re-entry helps only the selected cohort (Sections 5 and 6 ). The conditional-null result is theoretical; the findings on real streams, learned scores, adapter value, and response design are empirical. Together, they show that a monitor cannot be treated as a plug-in safeguard: both its statistical assumptions and the actions it triggers must be validated in the full adaptive system.

sections.heading: 2.1 Anytime-valid testing and conformal martingales
sections.text: Ville’s inequality ( Ville, 1939 ) bounds the probability that a nonnegative martingale started at one ever crosses a fixed threshold, the basis of anytime-valid testing. Vovk et al. (2003) test exchangeability online with conformal martingales, Fedorova et al. (2012) and Volkhonskiy et al. (2017) give the plug-in and inductive variants, and Vovk et al. (2021) reset the wealth on a fire for change-point detection, the rule this gate uses with the randomized p p -values of Vovk et al. (2022) . Shafer (2021) and Ramdas et al. (2023) frame the family as betting-based statistics valid under optional stopping. Later work extends the betting machinery ( Choe and Ramdas, 2026 ; Szabadváry, 2026 ) , tests exchangeability directly ( Saha and Ramdas, 2024 ; Ramdas et al., 2022 ) , and develops sequential change detectors from e-processes ( Shin et al., 2024 ; Bhattacharyya and Ramdas, 2026 ) . The conformal martingales studied here assume an exchangeable score sequence; other e-processes can target other nulls. We ask what the exchangeability premise is worth when the monitored learner produces the scores.

sections.heading: 2.2 Monitoring deployed models under shift
sections.text: Anytime-valid tests can track a deployed model’s risk ( Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2022 ) , extend to unlabeled streams through a secondary error model ( Amoukou et al., 2024 ) , bound running risk from few true labels ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , or reweight against covariate shift ( Prinster et al., 2025 ) . Appendix K reports our replay on the saved streams. Related work surveys heuristic drift detectors ( Gama et al., 2014 ) , gates adaptation on a detector ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and supplies the whiteness diagnostic used here ( Ljung and Box, 1978 ) . Those monitors watch a fixed model, a risk bound, or a covariate shift. Here the monitored score stream can inherit dependence from the forecast residuals, and overlap and adaptation can amplify it.

sections.heading: 2.3 Conformal prediction under dependence
sections.text: Conformal validity can tolerate bounded departures from exchangeability ( Barber et al., 2023 ) . Other methods adapt coverage under distribution shift ( Gibbs and Candès, 2021 ; Gibbs and Candès, 2024 ) , maintain it through change points ( Sun and Yu, 2025 ) , or accommodate serial dependence ( Xu and Xie, 2021 ; Xu and Xie, 2023 ; Oliveira et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2025a ) . Those methods repair the forecast’s own interval, while the premise at stake here is exchangeability of the monitor’s scores. Proposition 1 restates for the conditional null’s oracle score the overlapping-observations autocorrelation of forecast evaluation ( Hansen and Hodrick, 1980 ; Diebold and Mariano, 1995 ) and adds the non-exchangeability it implies; what this paper measures is its consequence for a monitor that shares its scores with the learner.

sections.heading: 2.4 Test-time adaptation of forecasters
sections.text: Frozen forecast foundation models ( Auer et al., 2025 ; Ansari et al., 2024 ; Ansari et al., 2025 ; Das et al., 2024 ; Woo et al., 2024 ) are deployed without gradient updates, and Meyer et al. (2025) document that their pretraining exposure to public streams is hard to establish. Wang et al. (2021) is the canonical test-time adaptation method, and Liang et al. (2025) survey the area. Error accumulation and collapse under continual adaptation motivate reset mechanisms ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Niu et al., 2023 ; Press et al., 2023 ; Lim et al., 2026 ) ; the weather divergences here instantiate that failure. Bar et al. (2024) instead drive adaptation with a betting martingale on the adapted model’s own statistic, the design whose premise this paper measures. For online forecasting, Pham et al. (2023) and Zhang et al. (2023) use immediate full reveal, a protocol criticized by Lau et al. (2025) and Wang et al. (2026) . Leakage-free reveal protocols appear in Zhao and Shen (2025) , Lau et al. (2025) , Kim et al. (2025) , Lee et al. (2025b) , and Dai et al. (2026) . Section 6 studies these settings, and we evaluate five released refiners on the same cells. Our adapter is the dynamic linear model of West and Harrison (1997) . Its fallback is an exponentially weighted average forecaster ( Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi, 2006 ) , with a fixed share in its first version ( Herbster and Warmuth, 1998 ) .

The fixed-construction null feeds i.i.d. synthetic scores through the gate’s own logic with no learner behind it. The no-parameter-drift simulation runs the complete pipeline on a fixed-design regression stream with i.i.d. residuals, 60 runs of 20,000 steps; its design is time-varying, so its ordered pairs are neither identically distributed nor exchangeable (Appendix A ). The original campaign runs four primary Kalman variants and two SGD baselines in every real-data cell. The Kalman variants are the ungated filter; the Huber-only variant; the full gate; and the fixed-cutoff variant, which uses only the spike check and no martingale. The Huber-only variant retains the martingale and spike classifier. A fire opens or restarts recovery and suppresses spike classification, but applies none of the three drift responses. Three exploratory single-component response ablations (soft reset, boost, override) complete the nine-configuration grid. Later sections add variants where they are used; Appendix A lists them all.

sections.heading: 4 Premise failure on the deployed score streams
sections.text: We run the gate on the five real streams under immediate reveal and count fires on clean replay at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 . All 135 clean runs of the three martingale-carrying variants fire at least once, and delayed reveal does not remove the pattern (Figure 2 ; Appendix C ). Figure 2: Clean-stream alarm census, summed over five streams and three seeds per backbone. Filled markers denote immediate reveal and hollow markers delayed reveal; connectors pair the same variant and backbone. Every plotted martingale-carrying variant fires repeatedly under both protocols. Totals establish firing; rate comparisons require exposure normalization. Appendix C reports per-run ranges and first-fire steps. Two diagnostic experiments locate the failure. The fixed-construction null fires in at most 1 of 60 runs, below the nominal reference 0.05 × 60 = 3 0.05\times 60=3 . This is an empirical calibration check; the deployed sliding-window gate has no formal Ville bound. The no-parameter-drift simulation fires in every one of its 60 runs, 33 to 42 times, the first fire 18 to 67 steps after warm-up ends (Appendix J ). In this finite synthetic check, the gate is quiet on i.i.d. input, so the pipeline’s own scores break the premise even though the data-generating parameters do not drift.

sections.heading: 4.1 Element-level isolation
sections.text: A second campaign of twenty-two variants holds the adaptive simulation’s elements one at a time over the same 60 seeds (Table 45 ; Appendix J lists each). Nineteen variants keep the campaign’s 500-step warm-up and default initialization. The eleven that learn R R online fire or cross in 60 of 60 runs. The eight that hold R R fixed fire or cross in 1 to 3 of 60. Online estimation of an unconverged R R is the feature shared by every variant that fires in all 60 runs. Four variants swap the gate for the classical no-reset wealth process of Section 3 , run in shadow. If the scores were exchangeable, Ville’s inequality would put the expected number of runs crossing 1 / α \nicefrac{{1}}{{\alpha}} at or below 3 of 60; it crosses in 60 of 60 with the scale learned and in 1 of 60 with it held, 3 of 60 on the permuted stream. These score processes violate the exchangeability assumption, so Ville’s bound does not apply. The element-level interventions attribute the excess crossings in this simulation to the convergence transient in the learned observation-noise estimate. The permuted stream makes the same point on an exchangeable input, where the complete pipeline still fires in 60 of 60 runs and the same pipeline with no hyperparameter learning in 1 of 60 (Appendix J ). The mechanism is visible in the score. Held fixed, the mean across the 96 coordinates of R R stays at 0.0079 0.0079 , about three times the true coordinate value 0.0025 0.0025 , and the mean score is about 30 30 , whereas a well-specified χ 96 2 \chi^{2}_{96} score has mean 96. Learned online, the same coordinate mean converges while the score climbs from 90.2 90.2 to 96.1 96.1 . Each new score then exceeds most of its calibration window, so the p p -values run small and dependent and both constructions read the convergence as drift. Neither longer-warm-up variant fires in any of its 60 runs, while Ljung-Box rejects at level 0.05 in 17 and 13 of 60 for the 2,000- and 5,000-step variants, respectively. Starting R R at its true value reduces firing to 2 of 60 runs, while Ljung-Box rejects in 58 of 60 (Table 45 ). Appendix J also reports the stricter 0.01 level. The firing in this simulation is therefore the estimate’s convergence transient.

sections.heading: 4.2 The frozen-scale variant on the real streams
sections.text: We next test this modification on the real streams. The variant holds R R at its warm-up value while λ \lambda and Q Q keep learning. It fires in 45 of 45 clean runs under each protocol, as the full gate does, so the convergence transient does not explain the real-stream firing (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: 4.3 The classical no-reset wealth process and origin overlap on real streams

If these scores were exchangeable, Ville’s inequality would put the expected count at or below 9. In all 180 runs, the marginal-uniformity and serial-dependence diagnostics show substantial departures from the joint i.i.d.-uniform premise. The sliding window and wealth reset are not necessary for crossing. The phenomenon is not unique to the block Kalman design. The SGD adapter’s own score stream crosses in 45 of 45 runs under each protocol. Thinning the saved scores offline to stride 96 lowers the crossing fraction of run-offset pairs from 0.631 and 0.673 to 0.032 and 0.044 under the two reveals, a descriptive contrast since offsets of one run share its stream (Appendix D ). sections.heading: 5 Attribution of the damage to the soft reset and the protocol
sections.text: One transient in the weather stream anchors this section. It lands at steps 18,536 to 18,538 on every backbone and seed under immediate reveal. The full gate turns it into a divergence on two of three backbones on 3 of 3 seeds. TimesFM 2.5 survives every seed; the full gate finishes at 2.57–3.06, versus 0.36 for the ungated filter (Table 27 ). In an exploratory component-ablation campaign, the soft-reset variant alone reproduces the divergence on the same transient, on 3 of 3 seeds on TiRex and Chronos-2 (Figure 4 ; the divergences recur on the completed cache, Appendix B ). Figure 4: Weather transient under immediate reveal. (a) TiRex, seed 0: per-step MSE, guard termination (red × \times ), and fires (ticks). (b) Completed-cache maximum per-step MSE by variant and backbone. Under delayed reveal the full gate goes from 60 divergences to 2 over 450 runs (Appendix E ). It survives the transient on every backbone and seed, and it still has the worst MSE among the four primary Kalman variants there (Table 28 ). The three single-component variants each diverge in 2 of 450 delayed runs, at the full gate’s two weather spike cells. The delayed-reveal data therefore do not identify one component as the unique cause. Over twenty seeds per backbone on the clean weather stream, the soft-reset variant finishes above the ungated filter in 20 of 20 seeds on every backbone. It finishes above the full gate in 18, 14, and 13 of 20 paired seeds, while the boost and override variants finish below the full gate on every backbone (Table 29 ). Removing the soft reset alone from the full gate, with the recovery rule kept, removes the immediate-reveal divergence and most of the cost under both protocols. That variant finishes the clean weather cell at 0.136 to 0.434 under immediate reveal, where the full gate diverges or reaches 3.06, finishes below the full gate in 20 of 20 delayed seeds on every backbone, and diverges in 1 of 450 immediate runs against the full gate’s 60, and in 3 of 450 delayed runs against its 2 (Appendix E ). On this event, within this response design, the soft-reset-only variant reproduces the observed divergence and most of the measured damage, and removing the reset alone avoids most of that damage.

sections.heading: 6 Alternative monitors and adapter value
sections.text: The frozen backbone provides the reference for the adapter’s value (Appendix G ). Under diagnostic immediate reveal, the adapter gains on 12 of 15 cells but multiplies the frozen error 2.9 to 22 times on weather. Under composite coordinate and delayed reveal, it loses on 14 and 15 of 15 cells, with median gains of − 0.34 -0.34 and − 0.60 -0.60 (Appendix H ). As a third-party diagnostic, the ORCA residual refiner ( Dai et al., 2026 ) gains on all 12 non-weather cells in our evaluation, suggesting that the Kalman result is not universal. Different inputs and warm-up rules prevent a fair ranking. An offline oracle using the adjacent label recovers 84 to 95 percent of the frozen model’s error on four streams; the tested causal residual summaries recover at most 23 percent. Fixing the forgetting factor still yields negative median gain. Under causal reveal, the adapter’s post-change error is 0.16 to 0.73 of the frozen error off weather but 2.0 to 323 times it on weather (Appendix H ). The fixed cutoff remains within the shaded ± 0.05 \pm 0.05 band among survivors; two delayed-weather pairs diverge. The full gate reaches + 6.81 +6.81 on ETTm1; Appendix E gives all cells. In the selected 36 immediate-reveal runs where the ungated adapter has positive clean gain, excluding weather, the capped policy retains 0.96 of that gain under packet spikes, versus − 0.35 -0.35 for the ungated filter. This cohort does not establish general effectiveness. The full gate, fixed cutoff, and capped policy all lose under packet-level shifts and freezes. Appendix G reports the complete retention analysis and the exploratory frozen-backbone mixture. The fixed cutoff has no anytime-valid guarantee. Its median clean action rate is 34.0 percent, against a nominal 0.1 percent. Its survivor-only ratio stays within ± 0.05 \pm 0.05 on every stream, but two delayed-weather pairs diverge. Under the fixed 100-fold guard from step 200, adverse delayed totals (divergence or higher error) are 45/45 ungated, 22/45 Huber-only, 40/45 full gate, and 18/45 cutoff (Figure 5 ; Appendix E ). Two exploratory variants test response capping and detector thinning. Capping removes covariance reset and recovery re-entry; during each 50-step recovery window, it holds λ = 0.95 \lambda=0.95 and linearly decays the tenfold process-noise boost. It diverges in 1 of 450 immediate runs and no clean runs. Detector stride 96 lowers clean-run firing from 45/45 to 11/45 and 10/45 under immediate and delayed reveal, with 6/450 and 2/450 divergences (Tables 7 and 30 ). Within 960 steps at magnitude 1.0, the A = 400 A=400 e-detector alarms on frozen residuals in 28/45 runs, versus 0/45 clean twins and 0/45 adapter-residual runs. Frozen scores remain 14–17 times baseline through step 2,000. Over the full post-onset test block, the live stride-96 detector alarms in 43/45 runs under either reveal versus 8/45 clean twins; among detected runs, median actionable latencies are 405 and 501 steps ( Shin et al., 2024 ) . The signal improves detection, but hold and handover force a tradeoff between contamination robustness and genuine-change adaptation. Dependence leaves the detector’s average-run-length guarantee unjustified; Appendix L reports the negative short-window results. At 5 percent, packet freezes degrade the fixed cutoff on four non-weather streams ( + 1.72 +1.72 to + 13.76 +13.76 ); packet shifts degrade every tested ETTh2 variant (13/13) and all Kalman variants on ETTm1 and traffic. The spike check therefore does not prevent sustained-change damage: the prespecified composite fails on all three backbones (Table 35 , Figure 8 ).

sections.heading: 7 Implications and scope
sections.text: Proved. Overlap breaks exchangeability of oracle scores; disjoint origins restore it only for that scorer. Measured. On real streams, alarms occur on dependent, marginally nonuniform scores. Adaptation can amplify damage, and neither system improves prediction uniformly. Neither procedure has its nominal guarantee on these streams. Scope. Evidence covers one adapter, three backbones, five fixed paths, and horizon 96. Most cells use three seeds; the delayed-reveal clean-weather ablation uses 20 per backbone. A guarantee matters only when its assumptions hold for the deployed score process.

sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI to help interpret saved experimental outputs, draft the statement and proof of Corollary 1 in Appendix D , and edit the manuscript, including suggesting word choices. sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: Every final result replays the completed backbone-forecast cache. Appendix B records the earlier incomplete-cache campaign as a provenance audit, specifies the rule that selects completed reruns for the final record, and gives the dataset, split, normalization, model-release, seed, and configuration conventions. Appendix A specifies the adapter recurrence, reveal-time event order, gate, injectors, and synthetic nulls. Every number in the main text is stated with its cohort and traces to a saved result record or action log. The classical no-reset wealth process’s replays check the saved p p -values and crossings against an offline recomputation in every run, and the conditional-null variants use matched pre-treatment draws. The supplementary material contains the code for the main experiment families and the dependencies they require. Their configurations generate the primary settings, diagnostic experiments, and follow-up settings rather than one entry point per reported variant. The full codebase, saved result records, action logs, and completed forecast cache will be released upon publication. The external-refiner evaluation is reported as a third-party diagnostic and uses the released methods at their default settings. The weather and traffic streams are the long-horizon benchmark versions of Wu et al. (2021) , obtained from a maintained benchmark release, and carry no license identifier of their own. sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work uses five public forecasting benchmarks and three publicly released frozen forecast models, and it involves no human subjects and no personal data. Its subject is a deployed safety mechanism whose guarantee does not hold under the conditions studied here. We report that failure, its measured causes, constructive diagnostics, and response baselines. These results help practitioners avoid relying on the guarantee where its premise fails. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

sections.heading: Appendix A Experimental specifications
sections.text: Figure 1 draws the adaptation loop of Section 3 . The two synthetic nulls below sever that loop at the stream and at the learner. Adapter. The filter’s state holds a slope and an intercept per horizon, 192 entries for the 96-step horizon, and the frozen forecast enters through each horizon’s observation row [ f t , h ​ 1 ] [f_{t,h}\;\;1] , so the state dimension is set entirely by the forecast horizon. Every run starts from the same library defaults. After each non-skipped feedback packet, the hypergradient step on the innovation likelihood updates λ \lambda and the entries of Q Q and R R , so the filter’s own noise model tracks the stream it calibrates without a held-out validation split. Drift response and constants. On a fire the covariance is soft reset to 4 ​ P t 4P_{t} , the process noise is boosted tenfold with linear decay over a 50-step recovery window, and the effective forgetting factor is held at 0.95 throughout that window; at the weather event traced in Section 5 the boost multiplier is 9.6, and the logged process noise there is 2.0 × 2.0\times the ungated filter’s. Spike classification is suppressed while a window is open. The learned forgetting factor sits at its 0.90 floor on weather, where the override lengthens the memory, and at medians of 0.95 to 0.997 on the other four streams, where it shortens the effective memory to about 20 origins. The spike check clips an innovation whose score exceeds q q , the 0.999 quantile of χ 96 2 \chi^{2}_{96} (144.6), to Mahalanobis norm q \sqrt{q} , and skips the update above 3 ​ q 3q . The hypergradient step is Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) with step sizes 10 − 3 10^{-3} on λ \lambda and 10 − 2 10^{-2} on log ⁡ Q \log Q and log ⁡ R \log R , started at λ = 1 \lambda=1 , every entry of Q Q at 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and every entry of R R at 1, with λ \lambda kept in [ 0.90 , 1 ] [0.90,1] . The coordinates of Q Q and R R then adapt separately. The capped policy removes the covariance soft reset and disables recovery re-entry. It retains the full gate’s λ = 0.95 \lambda=0.95 override and tenfold process-noise boost with 50-step linear decay. A fire during an open recovery window is recorded but does not restart the window. The full gate without its soft reset retains re-entry. Contamination injectors. These interventions operate on the origin-horizon label array after overlapping labels have been formed; they do not first corrupt one timestamp-indexed sensor path and then slice it into labels. The same physical timestamp can therefore receive different values in different origin-horizon entries. The experiments measure corrupted feedback vectors and do not model a timestamp-consistent sensor failure. Each injector places its corruption at exactly round ⁡ ( f ​ T ) \operatorname{round}(fT) steps of the T T -step test block, for a contamination fraction f ∈ { 0.01 , 0.05 , 0.10 } f\in\{0.01,0.05,0.10\} . Each injection’s magnitude is set in robust units of the clean labels’ own scale, 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation computed per horizon. We call these packet interventions “spike,” “level shift,” and “freeze” throughout. Spike alters isolated uniformly chosen steps by six scale units, with a per-step random sign. Level shift applies a three-unit offset over one contiguous block, with one sign per horizon. Packet freeze holds one contiguous block at its onset value and carries no magnitude at all. sections.text: Datasets, splits, and scaling. Table 5 gives the exact origin ranges used by the main experiments. Indices are zero-based rolling-window origins. The split is chronological with nominal proportions 20:5:75. At both internal boundaries, 191 candidate origins are dropped so that a 96-step context and 96-step label cannot cross the boundary. The loader drops the date column, retains numeric columns in file order, and uses the last numeric column, the benchmark’s oil-temperature target channel, as the target. It performs no interpolation, imputation, or row deletion. Both the cached forecast and label are divided by the target’s standard deviation over the training rows, with no centering and a floor of one only if that standard deviation is at most 10 − 8 10^{-8} . Reported MSE is on this normalized scale; raw-scale MSE is obtained by multiplying by the squared recorded scale. All three models are frozen and receive only the last target channel from a 96-step context. Each emits a deterministic 96-step point forecast in float32, cached once per origin; the adapter subsequently operates in float64. CUDA is used when available, with CPU fallback. (2025) document is hard to establish for released time-series checkpoints. Possible pretraining overlap may nevertheless affect forecast quality and limits broader generalization. Every backbone forecast is computed once per origin and cached. Final tables and figures use the immutable completed-cache record. An earlier immediate-reveal campaign began before cache construction had finished; it is retained only as provenance and is not used for final results. Within each completed-cache campaign, runs that share a stream, backbone, and context receive byte-identical forecast inputs, and each contaminated run is paired with a clean twin built from the same cell. No value from the earlier incomplete-cache campaign appears in a final claim. We reran every cell of the six original variants on the completed cache, including the clean setting and all three injectors at 1, 5, and 10 percent. Of the 300 stream-setting-configuration ratios, 263 move by at most 0.01 and 280 by at most 0.05; divergence agrees in 297 cells, and differs by one run in the remaining three. The full gate’s weather divergence recurs in every corresponding rerun. The largest ratio changes are listed in Table 11 , and Tables 9 and 10 verify the main spike, freeze, and shift evaluations on the completed cache. Figure 4 (b) and the twenty-seed analysis in Table 29 likewise use completed-cache records. Every saved record carries the complete experimental configuration, including the feedback protocol, gate settings, and contamination settings. Records from different protocols or gate configurations are kept separate. The released provenance record keeps the earlier campaign separate from the completed-cache evidence. Three seeds cover every cell. Seeds are Monte Carlo replicates conditional on each fixed cached stream. Each gated run initializes its conformal tie-break generator from the run seed. Matched clean and contaminated cells with the same seed therefore use the same tie-break sequence over their common scored prefix. Contamination uses a separate child generator. On clean streams the ungated and fixed-cutoff variants reproduce across seeds, agreeing to eight significant figures, because neither consumes a randomized p p -value. The gated variants vary. The full gate’s clean weather runs on TiRex finish at 80.6, 75.4, and 76.4 across seeds 0, 1, and 2, where the ungated filter finishes at 2.032 in all three. Three seeds are a coarse resolution for any per-cell rate, and every pooled statistic in this paper carries its raw counts. Every degradation ratio in this paper, main text and appendix alike, follows ( 3 ). For a given variant, stream, contamination kind, and fraction, each of the three backbones times three seeds gives one pair, a contaminated run and its twin. A pair enters the mean only when both runs finished without crossing the divergence guard, which truncates a run once its cumulative MSE exceeds 100 times the seasonal-naive reference’s cumulative MSE, floored at 10 − 4 10^{-4} , checked from step 200 on, and at once on a non-finite state. This operational guard was fixed before the runs. Because a triggered run is truncated, the saved records cannot support a higher-threshold sensitivity analysis without rerunning the affected cells; no such analysis is claimed. A ratio where fewer than nine of nine pairs survive carries an explicit [ n / 9 ] [n/9] mark. Divergence itself is reported as its own outcome wherever it occurs, never folded into a mean. All verdicts, exclusion rules, and contamination severities were fixed before the runs. The composite gate rule requires the gated variant to beat the ungated variant, per contamination kind, on at least three of five comparable stream cells. Cells where the ungated variant itself degrades by less than five percent are excluded as incomparable, and the gate passes only if every evaluated kind passes. Measured against that rule, the gate fails on three of three backbones. The supplementary material contains the code for the main experiment families and the dependencies they require. The full codebase, immutable completed forecast cache, saved result records, and action logs will be released upon publication. Earlier incomplete-cache records are retained separately as provenance and are not used for final results.

sections.heading: Appendix D Classical no-reset replay and origin-overlap analyses
sections.text:
Two shadow variants rerun the deployed loop on the real streams and save every score, one with all three hyperparameters learning and one with the observation-noise scale held at its warm-up value. Both run in shadow, so the gate observes every score and acts on none. Across three backbones, five streams, three seeds, and two protocols the bundle holds 180 clean runs and 4,932,540 steps, of which 4,923,900 are scored, each of the 90 delayed-reveal runs spending its first 96 steps predict-only. An offline replay recomputes the deployed p p -values and the fire sequence from those raw scores and reproduces both exactly in 180 of 180 runs, so every number in Table 14 is measured on the score sequences the deployed gate itself saw. The classical no-reset wealth process keeps every score in its calibration set and uses the wealth of Algorithm 1 with no reset, at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 , so its log-wealth threshold is log ⁡ 20 \log 20 . If a cell’s score sequences were exchangeable, Ville’s inequality would limit the expected number of crossing runs to 2.25 per 45-run cell. No such premise is assumed for these observed streams. Every cell crosses in 45 of 45. The deployed gate’s first fire on the same streams has a median of 515 steps under immediate reveal and 138 under delayed with the scale learned, and 535 and 139 with it held, over the 45 runs of each variant and protocol. The classical no-reset wealth process’s pooled first crossing has a median of 528 and 138 steps with the scale learned and 776 and 139 with it held, so the medians coincide under delayed reveal and differ by 13 steps under immediate reveal with the scale learned. The level and the calibration length are the two settings the validity argument turns on, so both were swept on these same saved streams. The shadow variants apply no response, so the score stream does not depend on what the gate decided, and a gate configured differently and fed these scores would have seen exactly them. Over the 90 clean runs with the scale learned, pooling both protocols, the deployed gate fires in 90 of 90 at every calibration length of 100, 250, and 500 and at every level from 0.05 0.05 down to 10 − 6 10^{-6} . At 10 − 8 10^{-8} it still fires in 90 of 90 at lengths 100 and 250 and in 87 of 90 at 500. The classical no-reset wealth process crosses in 90 of 90 down to 10 − 6 10^{-6} and in 80 of 90 at 10 − 8 10^{-8} . The clean-stream firing is therefore not a property of the level or the window length this campaign chose, since a threshold of 10 8 10^{8} leaves it in place. The swept lengths span the range the adapter’s configuration admits, and the growing calibration set of the no-reset variant is the unbounded end of that same axis. In an exploratory, post hoc analysis, the betting family was swept on the same 90 streams at level 0.05 0.05 and length 250. The deployed mixture over the epsilon grid crosses in 90 of 90 and fires in 90 of 90, and a single fixed bet of 0.9 0.9 does the same. A fixed bet of 0.5 0.5 crosses in 43 and fires in 53 of 90, and a fixed bet of 0.1 0.1 crosses in 5 and fires in 5 of 90, near the nominal reference of 4.5. The betting family is therefore not immaterial. The exponent 0.1, the one that stays at its expected count, bets most on very small p p -values and loses wealth on every p p -value above 0.077, so on these streams, whose p p -values are small but rarely that small, its wealth collapses; at a pseudo-onset placed at 60 percent of each run its log-wealth sits 10,642 to 43,491 below the threshold of log ⁡ 20 \log 20 , a deficit that 960 steps cannot recover, since a calibration set of several thousand scores caps each step’s gain near 7. sections.heading: Appendix E Divergence counts by variant and protocol
sections.text: Three backbones, five streams, ten contamination settings, and three seeds give 450 runs per variant per protocol for each of the six original variants. Divergence counts fall sharply when the loop is made causal. Figure 7 reports the six original variants. Table 30 adds the nine later variants. The full gate goes from 60 divergences under immediate reveal to 2 under delayed reveal. Eight Kalman divergences remain under delayed reveal, two full gate, one ungated filter, three Huber-only, and two fixed cutoff. Seven of the eight belong to one stream and setting, the weather stream at seed 1 under the 5 percent spike injector, with the divergence guard triggered at exactly step 200. The eighth belongs to the Huber-only variant on ETTm1 under the packet-freeze injector, triggered at step 8,982. Divergence-inclusive sensitivity. For the 45 paired runs behind Figure 5 , an adverse outcome is either divergence of the contaminated run or, when both runs survive, a larger final MSE than its clean twin. Under immediate and delayed reveal, respectively, adverse outcomes occur in 42 and 45 runs for the ungated filter, 32 and 22 for Huber-only, 34 and 40 for the full gate, and 29 and 18 for the fixed cutoff. These counts include contaminated-run divergences of 0 and 1, 0 and 2, 6 and 2, and 0 and 2 in the same order; no clean-only run diverges. This sensitivity assigns no numerical loss to a truncated run and does not replace the separate divergence and survivor-only results. Four later variants extend the table. The frozen-scale variant diverges in 60 of 450 runs under immediate reveal and 2 of 450 under delayed reveal, matching the full gate on both, with the immediate divergences falling on TiRex and Chronos-2 alone. Its clean weather cell finishes at a median 84.8 on TiRex and 211.2 on Chronos-2, both on 3 of 3 diverged seeds, against the full gate’s 76.4 and 161.8 on the same cells. The capped-policy variant diverges in 1 of 450 immediate runs, at weather under the 10 percent spike injector on TiRex, and in none of its clean cells. It cuts boosted steps per run from per-backbone medians of 1,262 to 1,584 to medians of 950 to 1,200. On the four non-weather streams its clean test-block MSE lands between 23 percent below and 6 percent above the ungated filter’s on every backbone. The variant that leaves the spike check live during recovery diverges in 47 of 450, 15 on TiRex, 30 on Chronos-2, and 2 on TimesFM 2.5, with 5 of its 9 clean weather runs among them. Under delayed reveal both capped variants diverge in 2 of 450 runs, at the same two weather cells as the full gate, and in none of their clean cells. The three single-component variants complete the table. Under immediate reveal the soft-reset variant diverges in 60 of 450 runs, the full gate’s own count, the boost variant in 1, and the override variant in 0. Under delayed reveal each diverges in 2 of 450, at the two weather cells above, and in none of its clean cells. On the clean weather cell under delayed reveal, in the order TiRex, Chronos-2, and TimesFM 2.5, the soft-reset variant finishes at 0.98 to 1.03, 8.43 to 8.50, and 1.15 to 2.35. The boost variant finishes at 0.34 to 0.37, 5.62 to 5.69, and 0.69 to 0.72, and the override variant at 0.33 to 0.34, 2.65 to 2.90, and 0.65 to 0.72. The full gate finishes at 0.50 to 0.53, 8.32 to 9.14, and 1.18 to 1.23, and the ungated filter at 0.29, 5.75, and 0.52. On the four other clean streams the soft-reset variant’s test-block MSE sits 0.12, 0.19, 0.04, and 0.01 above the ungated filter’s on electricity, ETTh2, ETTm1, and traffic, means over nine runs, against 0.13, 0.20, 0.01, and 0.01 for the full gate, 0.15, 0.10, 0.00, and 0.00 for the boost variant, and 0.01, 0.02, 0.01, and − 0.01 -0.01 for the override variant. Tables 27 and 28 list the first three seeds of the clean weather cell for every variant under each protocol. Table 29 gives the paired per-seed differences from the ungated filter under delayed reveal over twenty seeds per backbone, seven variants rerun on that cell alone under the same configuration and the three variants added later over the same seeds. Over the twenty seeds the soft-reset variant’s mean excess over the ungated filter is 0.61, 3.57, and 1.37 on TiRex, Chronos-2, and TimesFM 2.5 against the full gate’s 0.23, 2.98, and 1.11, positive in 20 of 20 seeds for both variants. The soft-reset variant exceeds the full gate in the same seed in 18, 14, and 13 of 20 (two-sided sign test 0.0004, 0.12, and 0.26). sections.heading: Appendix G Adapter gain over the frozen backbone and its retention
sections.text: Every degradation ratio in the paper is taken to the ungated filter, so a reference variant that never adapts, the frozen backbone’s own forecast through the identity calibration, states what the adapter is worth and lets every other variant be read in units of that worth. The variant reads no label, so it is immune to label contamination, and one clean cell per backbone and stream is its reference for every cell. Gain is the quantity of ( 3 ), taken for the ungated filter’s clean run; retention reads every other variant’s run L L in units of that gain, with L ungated L_{\text{ungated}} the ungated filter’s clean run, retention = L frozen − L L frozen − L ungated , \text{retention}=\frac{L_{\text{frozen}}-L}{L_{\text{frozen}}-L_{\text{ungated}}}, (11) so one keeps the whole clean gain, zero is no better than never adapting, and a negative value is worse. Retention is undefined where the ungated filter has no gain, which excludes weather and every delayed cell; no run entering Table 36 diverged. sections.text: The composite coordinate reveal of Kim et al. (2025) and Lau et al. (2025) uses the packet in Table 3 . At reveal step r r , its horizon- h h block pairs the newly observed label with the forecast issued at r − h r-h , so that block’s lag is exactly h h . The first 96 steps are predict-only because the implementation forms a complete 96-block packet before an update. Immediate reveal instead uses the 96 future labels of origin r r , 95 of which also occur in the next 95 origins, whereas delayed reveal uses the complete label of origin r − 96 r-96 . All three updates use the state and predicted covariance at reveal step r r . All 96 composite rows forecast the same physical target time, so their forecast errors are strongly dependent. The implementation nevertheless models the innovation covariance across horizon blocks as diagonal. The results below therefore describe this composite diagonal-covariance update, not every coordinate-reveal estimator. A second variant widens each horizon’s block from [ f t , h ​ 1 ] [f_{t,h}\;\;1] to [ f t , h ​ 1 ​ r t − 1 ​ [ 1 ] ​ r t − h ​ [ h ] ​ r ¯ t ] [f_{t,h}\;\;1\;\;r_{t-1}[1]\;\;r_{t-h}[h]\;\;\bar{r}_{t}] , with r t = y t − f t r_{t}=y_{t}-f_{t} the frozen residual vector of origin t t as in Appendix D , so r t − j ​ [ j ] r_{t-j}[j] is the residual of the forecast made j j origins earlier for the label observed at t t , and r ¯ t \bar{r}_{t} is the mean of r t − j ​ [ j ] r_{t-j}[j] over j = 1 j=1 to 24 24 ; each is divided by its training-block root mean square and given a prior variance of 0.1. The features are therefore the freshest observed errors, where Dai et al. (2026) condition a residual predictor on the model’s input and output and wait for the full horizon. Both variants run as their own configurations, and the frozen backbone, the ungated filter, and the fallback mixture run under each; the gated variants are not wired to the composite coordinate reveal. The rule for the widened variant, fixed before the runs, asked for a clean gain of at least 0.10 over the frozen backbone on at least 10 of 15 cells under the composite coordinate reveal with no diverged seed. Under the composite coordinate reveal the adapter without features is worse than the frozen backbone on 14 of 15 cells, median gain − 0.34 -0.34 , from − 0.58 -0.58 on TiRex ETTh2 to + 0.04 +0.04 on Chronos-2 ETTm1. The loss holds in every horizon band, − 0.13 -0.13 at horizons 1 to 8, − 0.19 -0.19 at 9 to 24, − 0.26 -0.26 at 25 to 48, and − 0.34 -0.34 at 49 to 96 (Table 41 ). Delayed reveal gives − 0.60 -0.60 on 15 of 15 and immediate reveal + 0.25 +0.25 on 12 of 15. The widened variant trips the divergence guard in 85 of 90 clean seeds, at or before the guard’s first check at step 200 in 42 of 45 under delayed reveal and after 124 to 13,789 steps under the composite coordinate reveal, with a non-finite hyperparameter state at step 0 on ETTm1 in 12 seeds, and the five surviving seeds finish 2.1 to 28.5 times the frozen error, so the rule fails at 0 of 15. Wrapped in the fallback mixture the widened variant forecasts as the frozen backbone, median gain − 0.010 -0.010 and a regime ratio of 1.000. An offline oracle separates information from estimation. On each cell it fits, on the training block, a per-horizon affine correction of the frozen forecast, the same correction with the three fresh residual features, the same with all 96 lagged residuals, and a ceiling that conditions on the label adjacent to the target, the information immediate reveal supplies, and scores each on the test block against the frozen backbone (Table 42 ). The adjacent label recovers 84 to 95 percent of the frozen error on four streams and 53 to 57 percent on traffic. Everything causally available recovers at most 23 percent, reaches 0.10 on 4 of 15 cells with all 96 lags (TimesFM 2.5 traffic prints as 0.100 and sits at 0.0997), and is negative on weather with all lags; on ETTm1 the affine correction alone is worse than the frozen backbone by 5 to 11 percent. A ridge recursive least-squares fit of the same corrections at forgetting factor 0.999, run online under the composite coordinate reveal, stays within − 0.01 -0.01 to + 0.14 +0.14 of the frozen backbone on ETTh2, electricity, and traffic and becomes unstable on ETTm1 and weather, further still with the features, with no Kalman filter and no hyperparameter learning involved; its rule, fixed in advance as a gain of 0.10 on 10 of 15 cells, fails at 0 of 15. The adjacent label therefore carries enough information to account for the scale of the immediate-reveal gain, and the causal residual summaries tested here carry little on these streams; the oracle is a training-block fit and an offline recursion, so it bounds information and does not reproduce the live adapter’s estimation. Dai et al. (2026) report single-digit to 16 percent error reductions for a residual predictor on the same backbones and streams under the delayed full-horizon reveal, with a different horizon average, context, and normalization; the negative results here are for this adapter family. The adapter’s own forgetting is part of the mechanism for its distance from the oracle, and only part. Its learned forgetting factor sits at a median of 0.949 to 0.997 on the four non-weather streams and at the floor of 0.90 on weather, under immediate and composite coordinate reveal alike, an effective memory of 20 to 330 origins against 1,000 at 0.999, and the hyperparameter learner moves it by less than 0.02 between the two reveals on every cell (Table 39 ). sections.heading: Appendix I ORCA diagnostic and simplified ports, not head-to-head method rankings
sections.text: The adapter conclusion of Section 6 is measured on one adapter family. This appendix evaluates five released refiners on the same 15 cells, the same cached forecasts, origins, train-block scale, divergence guard, seeds, and reveals, against the same frozen reference. The five are the refiners evaluated in the released ORCA study ( Dai et al., 2026 ) : the ORCA residual refiner, simplified ports of ELF ( Lee et al., 2025b ) , of the output calibration of TAFAS ( Kim et al., 2025 ) , and of DSOF ( Lau et al., 2025 ) , and its ridge baseline from the context and base forecast to the residual. Every hyperparameter uses its released default. The collection phase buffers 3,000 training snapshots and, for the TAFAS and DSOF ports, 300 validation snapshots before the first fit. The ports keep less than the papers. The ELF port weights its learners by mean absolute error and starts without the seasonal-naive learner, the TAFAS port keeps the output calibration module alone and drops the input calibration and the periodicity-aware schedule, and the DSOF port keeps the fast residual student and the slow replay stream; the optional confidence router, off at its released default, stays off in every port. All five adapt on complete horizon-length targets only. Each cell is one stride-one stream of origins, the training block, the validation block, and the test block, in order. At every origin the refiner first maps the cached point forecast and the 96-step context to its refined forecast, and then receives every snapshot whose closure step is the current step; a snapshot is the context, the cached forecast, the refiner’s own earlier forecast, and the full 96-step label of one origin. Warm-up origins close 96 steps after issue under every reveal, so the three reveals of a cell share their warm-up exactly. Test origins close at issue under the immediate reveal, which exposes their complete labels noncausally, and 96 steps after issue under the composite coordinate and delayed reveals. The refiners consume complete labels only, so the composite coordinate and delayed reveals carry identical information for them; the coordinate lane is a cross-process determinism check, and its refined forecasts reproduced the delayed lane’s bit for bit on 225 of 225 runs. Causality is checked from the closure delays every record carries; a second check fails any refiner whose forecasts reproduce the frozen backbone exactly, one that never trained. The ELF, TAFAS, and ridge refiners draw no random number, so their three seeds reproduce one forecast exactly on every cell under every reveal, and each of their cells is one run; the ORCA and DSOF refiners differ across seeds everywhere. The refiners warm on the training and validation blocks with the same 96-step closure, where the Kalman variants other than the warmed configuration use only the training block with each label fed at once; the refiners therefore hold the validation block’s labels before the test block, those Kalman variants never see them, and no variant sees a test label before its closure. The refined test-block forecasts pass through the same divergence tracker and cumulative score as every other variant, and a non-finite forecast is scored as it stands; none occurred in the 675 runs. The rule was fixed before the campaign ran. It passes if the ORCA refiner’s clean gain over the frozen backbone is at least 0 on at least 10 of the 12 non-weather cells under the delayed reveal, with three seeds on every cell and no diverged or non-finite seed. Under a pass, a published black-box adapter recovers value under the causal reveal on these streams at this horizon and context, so the loss of Section 6 is a property of the Kalman adapter family. Under a fail, at released defaults, on these backbones, streams, horizon, and context, the strongest cited black-box adapter also loses to the frozen backbone under the causal reveal, so the loss extends beyond the Kalman adapter. The same count for the other four variants, the immediate-minus-delayed difference per variant, and each variant’s per-cell delta against the Kalman variants are readings. The rule passes. The ORCA refiner’s median gain is at or above 0 on 12 of the 12 non-weather cells under the delayed reveal, from 0.05 to 0.29, pooled 0.14 over the 15 cells, with no diverged seed (Table 44 ). The gains are medians over three seeds; every seed of the ORCA refiner is at or above 0 on the 12 non-weather cells, the lowest at 0.05. The per-seed records are retained for release upon publication. The ELF, TAFAS, and ridge rows carry no seed spread because their three seeds reproduce one forecast. By the reading fixed before the campaign, the pass scopes the loss of Section 6 to the Kalman adapter family on these cells, at this horizon and context, under these reveals and defaults; the threats below name what the evaluation does not separate from family. The other four variants are readings. The no-parameter-drift simulation (Section 4 ) runs the full pipeline, the block Kalman filter, its online hyperparameters, the calibration window, the martingale, and the drift response, on a fixed-design regression stream with i.i.d. residuals and no parameter drift. Each stream’s per-step forecast pattern is a slowly varying sinusoid and its labels add i.i.d. Gaussian noise. The design is time-varying, so the ordered forecast and label pairs are neither identically distributed nor exchangeable. It uses 60 independent runs of 20,000 steps each, with a 500-step warm-up before the gate begins scoring. Every one of the 60 runs fires at least once. Fires per run range from 33 to 42, with a mean of 37.9. sections.heading: Appendix K E-detector replay
sections.text: Sequential e-detectors offer change detection under an average-run-length guarantee ( Shin et al., 2024 ) , so a natural question is whether swapping the martingale for a detector carrying that guarantee repairs the deployed premise. We built Shiryaev-Roberts ( Shiryaev, 1963 ; Roberts, 1966 ) and CUSUM ( Page, 1954 ) e-detectors from the deployed betting family and replayed them on the saved p p -value streams of the 405 saved clean gated runs. Those 405 streams cover six variants under immediate reveal (the Huber-only variant, the full gate, the SGD surrogate, and the three single-component variants) and three under delayed reveal (the Huber-only variant, the full gate, and the SGD surrogate), each over five streams, three backbones, and three seeds. The replay first reproduces the saved fire trajectory exactly in 405 of 405 runs, so the detectors read the same evidence the deployed gate read. Both detectors then alarm in all 405 of those streams at every threshold A ∈ { 10 3 , 10 4 , 10 5 } A\in\{10^{3},10^{4},10^{5}\} . The main text’s 135 immediate-reveal runs of the three martingale-carrying variants are 135 of 135 among them. Over those same 135 runs at A = 10 4 A=10^{4} the Shiryaev-Roberts detector produces 193, 320, and 1,464 alarms per run at the minimum, median, and maximum. For intuition only, the ratios T / A T/A range from 1.3 to 5.2 over these stream lengths. They are heuristic reference scales: the average-run-length guarantee concerns the first false alarm and does not bound alarm counts after restarts. In the two synthetic null checks below, the observed alarm behavior remains within the stated reference scales. On i.i.d. p p -value streams the restarted alarm counts stay at or below the corresponding T / A T/A reference at every threshold and stream length. This is not a formal bound on restarted counts. On i.i.d. scores passed through the deployed calibration window from an empty start, the Shiryaev-Roberts detector alarms in 15 of 30 runs at A = 10 4 A=10^{4} with at most 2 alarms per run, against the reference value T / A = 2.0 T/A=2.0 . These e-detector instantiations therefore inherit the invalidity of the deployed p p -value stream. A remedy must either restore exchangeability for this conformal construction or replace it with evidence valid under a dependence-aware null. E-processes that test exchangeability directly ( Ramdas et al., 2022 ) can measure whether a candidate remedy has done so. A classical detector calibrated under dependence asks the same question from outside the betting family. A two-sided Page CUSUM ( Page, 1954 ) with drift 0.5 runs on each run’s standardized scores, its threshold set on the first 6,000 scored steps of the same run in two ways, by a moving-block bootstrap ( Künsch, 1989 ) of that reference at block lengths 1, 96, and 500, and by rescaling the increments with a Newey-West estimate ( Newey and West, 1987 ) of the reference’s long-run variance at bandwidths 96, 250, and 500 against simulated i.i.d. paths. Both calibrations fail in finite samples in ways measured on i.i.d. data at this ratio of reference to monitoring length. The bootstrap of a short reference is anti-conservative for a maximum statistic (0.34 and 0.62 of 100 i.i.d. runs alarm at blocks 96 and 500), and the Bartlett estimate runs low when the bandwidth is a large fraction of the reference (0.25 and 0.43 at bandwidths 250 and 500). Only block length 1, the i.i.d. calibration, and bandwidth 96 hold within 0.15 there (0.04 and 0.11), and bandwidth 96 also stays at or below 0.01 on AR(1) and 96-term moving-sum synthetic streams. The reference segments carry a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.88 to 0.98 and an integrated autocorrelation time of 11 to 62 steps, and the long-run standard deviation at bandwidth 96 runs at a median 6.1 times the reference’s. On the 180 saved streams the i.i.d. calibration alarms in 180 of 180 at a median of 167 steps into monitoring, and the dependence-calibrated detector in 144 of 180 at a median of 5,076 steps, 36 of 36 on electricity, ETTm1, traffic, and weather and 0 of 36 on ETTh2, identically under both protocols and both scale variants. On the SGD adapter’s 90 streams it alarms in 78 of 90, 6 of 18 on ETTh2. A detector built to absorb dependence of the reuse length still alarms on four of five streams, and the stream it holds is one of the two on which the adapter’s horizon-1 term never crossed (Table 19 ); the settings whose i.i.d. calibration fails are retained for release upon publication as a sensitivity. A closely related published monitor is WATCH ( Prinster et al., 2025 ) , a weighted conformal test martingale that freezes its calibration set once a secondary martingale on the covariates alone detects a shift and thereafter weights every calibration p p -value by an online density ratio between calibration and target covariates. Replaying it needs the covariate each score was computed under, so twelve summary features of every origin’s context are rebuilt from the data on the split the streams were saved on. Four monitors then run on every saved clean run at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 with the composite jumper and no wealth reset. They are the plain conformal test martingale on the scores, the covariate martingale, WATCH with adaptation at the covariate process’s threshold of 20, and the same weighted procedure with adaptation forced at a 250-step burn-in (Table 47 ). On the 180 saved shadow runs, the learned-scale and frozen-scale shadow variants under both protocols, every monitor crosses 1 / α \nicefrac{{1}}{{\alpha}} in 180 of 180, whereas Ville’s inequality bounds the expected number of crossing runs under the null by 9. The plain wealth process crosses at a median step of 25; WATCH crosses at the same median step with a higher peak, 7,339 against 3,096 in log-wealth. The covariate wealth process crosses in every run at a median step of 44, so adaptation triggers in 180 of 180 runs between steps 20 and 78. WATCH had already crossed before reweighting could act in 141 runs; with adaptation forced at step 250, it had crossed in all 180. After adaptation the density-ratio classifier separates the calibration and target covariates almost perfectly on three streams, the weights’ effective sample size falling to a median of 1.0 to 1.2 calibration points on electricity, ETTh2, and traffic against 57 on ETTm1 and 16 on weather, and the weighted martingale keeps growing. On the SGD adapter’s 78 aligned shadow streams, every monitor crosses in 78 of 78. WATCH crosses at a median step of 40 and before adaptation in 37 of 78 runs. The 12 traffic streams of that bundle’s TiRex and Chronos-2 runs, saved with 12,912 to 13,009 test steps against the covariates’ 13,014, fail the alignment check and are excluded from every count. A marginal covariate change with the conditional law fixed, which weighted conformal monitoring is built to absorb, is not what breaks these streams. The covariates do shift at once and almost completely, but reweighting the calibration set leaves the score wealth process crossing everywhere. The covariate representation, the adaptation trigger, and the burn-in are this paper’s choices, so the replay tests whether reweighting this representation rescues these streams and leaves WATCH under every configuration untested. sections.heading: Appendix L Firing and response under a sustained regime change
sections.text: Reducing detector exposure and changing the response alter clean-stream firing in different ways, so this section tests whether the resulting variants remain responsive to a change the gate should find. A regime-shift injector moves every label from a deterministic onset at 60 percent of the test block to its end by a fixed sign and magnitude of 1.0 or 3.0 in robust-scale units. This follows the level-shift convention and defines a separate configuration for each magnitude and protocol. The every-origin variants are the ungated filter, full gate, capped policy, fixed cutoff, shadow variant, and full gate without its soft reset. Together with the detector-stride-96 pair, they run over five streams, three seeds, and three backbones: 45 runs per variant, magnitude, and protocol, with a clean cell beside each as background. Of the 1,440 regime records, 1,428 enter; the 12 excluded are the full gate’s immediate-reveal weather runs, which diverge at the transient of step 18,537 before the onset at 23,627. We fixed two summaries before running the study (Table 48 ). First, per variant and magnitude, the fraction of runs whose first post-onset fire lands within 96 steps of the onset against the fraction of background gaps within 96 steps, the background being the run’s own pre-onset inter-fire gaps pooled with its clean twin’s; a variant that fires after the onset no more often than its background does shows no onset-specific response under this heuristic. Second, the post-onset fed-label MSE against the ungated filter on the same cell, with the pre-onset ratio as the check that the variants agreed before the change, which they do to within 0.88 to 1.16. The firing and background fractions use different sampling units, so this comparison is descriptive and is not a power test. Under this heuristic analysis, the only deployed fraction above its background reference after rounding is 0.54 against 0.53 for the immediate-reveal full gate at magnitude 1.0. At the larger magnitude, its first fire lands within 96 steps in 0.51 of runs against a background of 0.53. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.07038v1 [cs.LG] 04 Oct 2026 The Premise Is the Problem: Exchangeability Failure in Self-Monitored Test-Time Adaptation Weijia Han University of Washington Seattle, USA wh73@uw.edu Lisha Qu University of Washington Seattle, USA lishaq@uw.edu Zhenda Li Independent Researcher Liying Liang Independent Researcher Abstract Modern forecasting models are often updated after deployment so they can respond to changing data. These updates can also make predictions worse, so practical systems need a reliable monitor that can detect harmful changes and trigger protection. A natural design is to monitor the same prediction errors that guide the updates. This paper asks whether the statistical guarantee behind such a monitor remains valid when monitoring and adaptation use the same feedback. We study this question in multi-step time-series forecasting. We show that overlapping targets and dependence in forecast errors can break a key assumption required by the guarantee. The monitor may then raise alarms even when no harmful change has occurred, and its response can further damage prediction quality. We also find that adaptation can hide sustained changes from its own monitor, while the original frozen model retains a clearer signal. These results expose a basic failure mode in self-monitored adaptation. They show why reliable deployment requires checking the monitor’s assumptions, comparing adaptation with the frozen model under realistic feedback, and limiting the effect of every protective response. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Self-monitored adaptation and the label-reuse mechanism; the stream is illustrative and the callouts summarize Section 4.3 . Consecutive 96-step labels share 95 of their 96 entries, so the oracle score is a moving sum. On a conditional null with the scorer held at the truth, reuse changes the classical no-reset wealth process from 2 or 3 of 60 crossings to 58 or 59 of 60; the Ville guarantee applies only when fresh labels are used. Appendix A specifies every component. Time-series foundation models forecast many steps ahead and are deployed frozen ( Auer et al., 2025 ; Ansari et al., 2025 ; Das et al., 2024 ) . Test-time adaptation corrects their forecasts from newly revealed labels ( Lee et al., 2025b ; Dai et al., 2026 ) , but learning from a corrupted or shifting stream can cause harm. Such an adaptive system therefore needs a monitor for protective action. Conformal test martingales offer an appealing guarantee for such a monitor. On an exchangeable score sequence the wealth crosses 1 / α 
icefrac{{1}}{{\alpha}} with probability at most α \alpha , uniformly in time. The adapter’s own scores are a readily available monitoring signal, so the natural design lets one score stream both drive the updates and police them (Figure 1 ). We call this self-monitored adaptation. This paper asks whether the guarantee survives that feedback loop. The question matters because the bounded probability of any false alarm is the reason to prefer such a gate over a heuristic threshold. A false alarm can trigger a response that damages the adapter. We study a block Kalman adapter applied to three frozen backbones: TiRex, Chronos-2, and TimesFM 2.5. We evaluate it on five public streams: ETTh2, ETTm1, weather, electricity, and traffic ( Zhou et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2021 ) . The main campaign uses immediate and delayed reveal. Targeted analyses use composite coordinate and stride-96 feedback. We count fires on clean replay and under injected contamination, separate the elements of the loop with synthetic nulls, replay the classical growing-calibration, no-reset wealth process on saved scores, build a conditional null that changes only the reuse of labels across overlapping horizons, and evaluate the adapter against the frozen backbone under deployable feedback. Because the deployed gate’s sliding calibration window and wealth resets make it heuristic, the classical replay is its formal audit. We recorded a decision rule before running each campaign. Later response, fallback, and frozen-residual studies were exploratory follow-ups and are labeled as such. We report every outcome, including a failed first design, and connect a classical dependence pattern to the loss of validity that occurs when an exact sequential test is applied outside its exchangeability null, and to damage from the resulting response. We make four contributions. • Failure of the statistical premise. We prove that reusing overlapping forecast labels can make even a correctly specified score sequence non-exchangeable, so the classical anytime-valid guarantee does not apply. In a controlled null, reuse raises crossings from 2 or 3 of 60 to 58 or 59 of 60; spacing origins one horizon apart restores validity for the truth-held scorer (Section 4 ; Appendix D ). • Evidence on real streams. Frozen-backbone residuals also cross without a learner, so adaptation is not necessary for the observed alarms. Using disjoint forecast origins greatly reduces crossings, but this real-stream comparison is descriptive and does not establish a Ville bound (Section 4.3 ; Appendix D ). • Value and limits of adaptation. The adapter absorbs a sustained change within one horizon, while the frozen residual remains elevated and can support later detection. Under two deployable feedback protocols, however, the adapter loses to the frozen backbone in 29 of 30 backbone–stream evaluations (Section 6 ). • Consequences of intervention. Detecting a change and responding safely are separate problems. The tested responses can reproduce divergence, act too often on clean data, or fail under sustained contamination; removing reset and re-entry helps only the selected cohort (Sections 5 and 6 ). The conditional-null result is theoretical; the findings on real streams, learned scores, adapter value, and response design are empirical. Together, they show that a monitor cannot be treated as a plug-in safeguard: both its statistical assumptions and the actions it triggers must be validated in the full adaptive system. 2 Related work 2.1 Anytime-valid testing and conformal martingales Ville’s inequality ( Ville, 1939 ) bounds the probability that a nonnegative martingale started at one ever crosses a fixed threshold, the basis of anytime-valid testing. Vovk et al. (2003) test exchangeability online with conformal martingales, Fedorova et al. (2012) and Volkhonskiy et al. (2017) give the plug-in and inductive variants, and Vovk et al. (2021) reset the wealth on a fire for change-point detection, the rule this gate uses with the randomized p p -values of Vovk et al. (2022) . Shafer (2021) and Ramdas et al. (2023) frame the family as betting-based statistics valid under optional stopping. Later work extends the betting machinery ( Choe and Ramdas, 2026 ; Szabadváry, 2026 ) , tests exchangeability directly ( Saha and Ramdas, 2024 ; Ramdas et al., 2022 ) , and develops sequential change detectors from e-processes ( Shin et al., 2024 ; Bhattacharyya and Ramdas, 2026 ) . The conformal martingales studied here assume an exchangeable score sequence; other e-processes can target other nulls. We ask what the exchangeability premise is worth when the monitored learner produces the scores. 2.2 Monitoring deployed models under shift Anytime-valid tests can track a deployed model’s risk ( Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2022 ) , extend to unlabeled streams through a secondary error model ( Amoukou et al., 2024 ) , bound running risk from few true labels ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , or reweight against covariate shift ( Prinster et al., 2025 ) . Appendix K reports our replay on the saved streams. Related work surveys heuristic drift detectors ( Gama et al., 2014 ) , gates adaptation on a detector ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and supplies the whiteness diagnostic used here ( Ljung and Box, 1978 ) . Those monitors watch a fixed model, a risk bound, or a covariate shift. Here the monitored score stream can inherit dependence from the forecast residuals, and overlap and adaptation can amplify it. 2.3 Conformal prediction under dependence Conformal validity can tolerate bounded departures from exchangeability ( Barber et al., 2023 ) . Other methods adapt coverage under distribution shift ( Gibbs and Candès, 2021 ; Gibbs and Candès, 2024 ) , maintain it through change points ( Sun and Yu, 2025 ) , or accommodate serial dependence ( Xu and Xie, 2021 ; Xu and Xie, 2023 ; Oliveira et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2025a ) . Those methods repair the forecast’s own interval, while the premise at stake here is exchangeability of the monitor’s scores. Proposition 1 restates for the conditional null’s oracle score the overlapping-observations autocorrelation of forecast evaluation ( Hansen and Hodrick, 1980 ; Diebold and Mariano, 1995 ) and adds the non-exchangeability it implies; what this paper measures is its consequence for a monitor that shares its scores with the learner. 2.4 Test-time adaptation of forecasters Frozen forecast foundation models ( Auer et al., 2025 ; Ansari et al., 2024 ; Ansari et al., 2025 ; Das et al., 2024 ; Woo et al., 2024 ) are deployed without gradient updates, and Meyer et al. (2025) document that their pretraining exposure to public streams is hard to establish. Wang et al. (2021) is the canonical test-time adaptation method, and Liang et al. (2025) survey the area. Error accumulation and collapse under continual adaptation motivate reset mechanisms ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Niu et al., 2023 ; Press et al., 2023 ; Lim et al., 2026 ) ; the weather divergences here instantiate that failure. Bar et al. (2024) instead drive adaptation with a betting martingale on the adapted model’s own statistic, the design whose premise this paper measures. For online forecasting, Pham et al. (2023) and Zhang et al. (2023) use immediate full reveal, a protocol criticized by Lau et al. (2025) and Wang et al. (2026) . Leakage-free reveal protocols appear in Zhao and Shen (2025) , Lau et al. (2025) , Kim et al. (2025) , Lee et al. (2025b) , and Dai et al. (2026) . Section 6 studies these settings, and we evaluate five released refiners on the same cells. Our adapter is the dynamic linear model of West and Harrison (1997) . Its fallback is an exponentially weighted average forecaster ( Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi, 2006 ) , with a fixed share in its first version ( Herbster and Warmuth, 1998 ) . 3 The online learner and the gate under test The adapter. Algorithm 1 in Appendix A gives the complete state transition, including the first-score convention and the classical no-reset process used in Section 4.3 . The gate. A conformal test martingale ( Vovk et al., 2003 ; Vovk et al., 2021 ; Ville, 1939 ; Shafer, 2021 ; Ramdas et al., 2023 ) runs on the scores, with the randomized conformal p p -value of Vovk et al. (2022) and a fixed 19-point mixture of power martingales as its wealth (Algorithm 1 ). The sliding calibration window, the wealth reset, and the learned covariance each depart from the classical construction, so this gate carries no proven Ville bound of its own. Section 4.3 replays the textbook version, the same p p -value over a calibration set that grows to hold every score and the same wealth with no reset. Its Ville bound applies only when the score sequence satisfies the required null. We therefore call it the classical no-reset wealth process when replaying observed scores. Throughout the paper, we say that the gate fires , the no-reset process crosses , and an e-detector alarms . The spike check runs only on a step with no fire and no open recovery window, and the three response components act together on a fire (Appendix A ). Feedback protocols. Let o o be a forecast origin and r r a physical reveal step. At each r r , the adapter predicts the current origin, then evaluates any available feedback using the state and covariance predicted at r r ; it does not restore issue-time state. Immediate reveal uses the complete packet from o = r o=r , an upper-information diagnostic unavailable in deployment. Delayed reveal uses the packet from o = r − 96 o=r-96 . Composite coordinate reveal ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Lau et al., 2025 ) combines the newly observed coordinate from each earlier origin; all 96 rows concern the same physical target time. The fourth protocol is the feedback-stride-96 protocol : every origin is forecast and evaluated for MSE, but only every 96th delayed packet produces a gate score and adapter update. It therefore changes both the learner’s feedback and the gate’s exposure. A separate detector-stride-96 variant updates the adapter from every feedback packet but sends only every 96th score to the wealth process. Appendix A defines both variants explicitly. Two shadow variants, one learning the observation-noise vector R R and one holding it, save the filter’s scores under the first two protocols while the gate acts on nothing (Section 4.3 ). Overlap breaks exchangeability of oracle scores; disjoint origins restore it only for that scorer. Measured. On real streams, alarms occur on dependent, marginally nonuniform scores.
